listening.title: City Cycle-Skills Course Enquiry
listening.focus: paraphrase, linked ideas, corrected details, and clear comparisons
listening.script:
Maya: Good morning, Riverside Community Centre, Maya speaking. How can I help you?
Jon: Good morning. I'm calling about the city cycle-skills course. I saw a poster for beginners and I'd like to join the next group.
Maya: Great. We have a new four-week course starting next month. It's designed for adults who haven't cycled for a long time or want more confidence on roads.
Jon: That's exactly me. I haven't ridden since school. When does it meet?
Maya: The sessions are on Saturday mornings, from 9 to 11, at Riverside Park. Actually, sorry, let me correct that — we moved them to Sunday mornings, same time, because of park maintenance on Saturdays.
Jon: Sunday 9 to 11, got it. Where exactly in the park?
Maya: By the south entrance, near the café. We provide bikes, but you can bring your own if you prefer. The fee is £40 for the whole course, and that includes bike hire, a safety check, and a printed guide to take home.
Jon: That's reasonable. Do I need any special equipment?
Maya: Just comfortable clothes and closed shoes. We lend helmets and lights if you need them. Also, you don't need to be very fit — we start with basic control in a quiet area before going on short local roads.
Jon: Good to know. Is the course popular?
Maya: Yes, last term's attendance summary was very positive. Weekday evening groups had about 12 people on average, but weekend morning groups were larger, around 20, and had better completion rates.
Jon: So weekends are busier but more people finish?
Maya: Exactly. People find it easier to attend regularly on weekends.
Jon: How do I sign up?
Maya: I can send you the online registration form by email. You'll need to complete it and bring photo ID to the first session. We also ask you to arrive 15 minutes early for a quick bike fitting.
Jon: Perfect. My email is jon dot harper at mail dot com.
Maya: Thanks, Jon. I'll send that today, and you can reply if you have questions.

questions.title: Reason for calling
questions.prompt: Why is Jon contacting the centre?
options: To join a beginner cycling course
To hire a bike for the park
To complain about park maintenance
To apply for a job as instructor
questions.explanation: He says he saw a poster for beginners and wants to join the next group. Bike hire is offered as part of the course, not his reason for calling.

questions.title: Schedule correction
questions.prompt: What does Maya correct about the sessions?
options: They now run on Sunday mornings
They now start at 8 a.m.
They now meet at north entrance
They now last for three hours
questions.explanation: She first says Saturday then corrects to Sunday mornings due to maintenance. The time remains 9 to 11, so the 8 a.m. option is incorrect.

questions.title: Course fee includes
questions.prompt: What is included in the £40 fee?
options: Helmet purchase and lights
Bike hire, safety check and guide
Park café vouchers and repair kit
Insurance and fitness test
questions.explanation: Maya lists bike hire, a safety check and a printed guide as included. Helmets are lent, not sold, so purchase is wrong.

questions.title: Attendance comparison
questions.prompt: What does the attendance summary show?
options: They were smaller than weekday groups
They had lower completion rates
They were larger and finished more often
They met less regularly
questions.explanation: Weekend groups averaged 20 versus 12 on weekdays and had better completion rates. The lower completion option reverses this finding.

questions.title: Next step to enrol
questions.prompt: What must Jon do to enrol?
options: Pay in cash at the café
Complete a fitness test beforehand
Buy his own bicycle
Bring photo ID to first session
questions.explanation: Maya says he must complete the online form and bring photo ID to the first session. Paying at the café is never mentioned.

reading.title: Millbridge Voices Oral History Project
reading.focus: paraphrase, linked ideas, and distinguishing claims from evidence
reading.passage:
The town of Millbridge in northern England was once a centre for textile production. By the 1980s most mills had closed, and many workers moved to other jobs or left the area. Although official records list dates and employment numbers, they say little about daily life during this period of change. To fill this gap, Millbridge Library and the history department at Northfield University started an oral-recording project in January 2023.

The project, called Millbridge Voices, invites residents aged 70 and over to share memories in recorded interviews. Volunteers from the university and the local community carry out the interviews after a short training course on listening skills and recording equipment. Each interview lasts between 45 and 60 minutes and takes place in the library or, if preferred, in the participant's home. At first, the team planned to record all interviews automatically unless someone objected. After discussion with an ethics group, they changed to an opt-in system, where participants give clear written permission before any recording starts and can pause or delete sections at any time. This change reduced the number of recordings slightly but increased trust.

The organisers argue that the main value of the project is not simply collecting facts, but understanding how people interpreted events. For example, official reports describe the closure of the Bridge Mill in 1984 as an economic decision affecting 300 jobs. In her interview, 78-year-old Elena Alvarez, who worked there for 22 years, spoke less about the date and more about the quiet in the town afterwards and how neighbours supported each other with food and childcare. Her account, like many others, shows the social effects that do not appear in employment statistics.

Participation has grown steadily. In the first six months, 28 interviews were completed, mostly with former mill workers. In the next six months, the number rose to 41, including more women who had worked at home or in shops, and several people who had moved to Millbridge in the 1970s from Pakistan and India. The team notes that weekend sessions have higher attendance than weekday ones, and that interviews conducted at home tend to be longer, averaging 58 minutes compared with 46 minutes in the library. All recordings are stored in the library archive, with copies available online only when participants agree.

The project team now plans to use the material in schools and in a small exhibition next spring. They believe that listening to personal stories helps younger people connect with local history more directly than reading textbooks alone. If funding continues, they hope to extend the project to include residents in their 60s, whose memories of the town's regeneration in the 1990s are not yet recorded.

questions.title: Purpose of project
options: To replace official employment records
To record daily life missing from records
To celebrate the textile industry's success
To train students in recording equipment
questions.explanation: The passage says official records lack daily life details and the project fills that gap. Replacing records misstates its supplementary purpose.

questions.title: Permission system change
options: Recordings became automatic for everyone
Only library interviews are now allowed
Participants must give clear written permission first
Volunteers can delete recordings without asking
questions.explanation: The team moved from automatic recording to opt-in with clear written permission. Automatic recording was the earlier plan, not the current system.

questions.title: Organisers' main claim
questions.prompt: What do organisers claim is the main value?
options: Collecting exact dates of mill closures
Understanding how people interpreted events
Proving economic reports were incorrect
Recording Elena Alvarez's employment history
questions.explanation: They argue value is understanding interpretation, not just facts. Elena's account is an example illustrating that claim, not the claim itself.

questions.title: Interview length comparison
questions.prompt: What does the passage say about interviews?
options: Home interviews average longer than library ones
Weekday sessions had higher attendance
First six months had more interviews
Most recent participants were former mill workers
questions.explanation: Home interviews average 58 minutes versus 46 in the library. Weekday attendance was lower, so that distractor contradicts the data.

questions.title: Future extension inference
questions.prompt: What can be inferred about future recordings?
options: They will focus only on the 1980s
They will no longer be stored online
They will stop if schools lose interest
They may include people in their sixties
questions.explanation: The team hopes to extend to residents in their 60s if funding continues. There is no evidence they will limit focus to the 1980s.

findings.issue: The stem asks only what the attendance summary shows, while all four options use undefined They. It never identifies weekend groups as the subject of the larger/smaller/completion comparison. The intended index2 is supported only after supplying that missing subject. Ask explicitly how weekend morning groups compare with weekday evening groups, and describe completion rates rather than groups finishing more often.

Museum tour times are labelled daily while Monday is closed. Daily can reasonably mean each open day, but on opening days is clearer. The mixed family-ticket/individual-visitor share denominator could also be labelled more explicitly.
